answer: Size solar from all twelve months on your bill, not from one bill. The default Lahore home uses {{out.annual_units|int}} units a year: that divided by one kW's yearly output is {{out.kw_annual|2}} kW, rounded up to {{out.panels|int}} panels = {{out.installed_kw|2}} kW. A single bill would suggest anything from {{out.kw_from_low_bill|2}} kW ({{out.low_month|raw}}) to {{out.kw_from_high_bill|2}} kW ({{out.high_month|raw}}).
how: Year: {{out.annual_units|int}} units ÷ {{out.pvout_year|int}} units per kW a year in {{out.city_name|raw}} = {{out.kw_annual|2}} kW. System tested: {{out.kw|2}} kW, rounded up to {{out.panels|int}} panels × {{out.panel_w}} W = {{out.installed_kw|2}} kW, making {{out.solar_year|int}} units a year. Hardest month: {{out.peak_month|raw}}, {{out.peak_units|int}} units ÷ {{out.peak_pvout|1}} units per kW = {{out.kw_peak|2}} kW. Each month, solar = system kW × that month's units per kW; used straight from the panels = the smaller of solar and {{out.day_share|pct}} of the month's units ({{out.self_used_year|int}} units a year); the rest of your use is bought from the grid ({{out.grid_units_year|int}} units) and the rest of the solar is exported: {{out.export_units_year|int}} units × {{out.buyback_rs|rs2}} = {{out.export_credit_rs|rs}}.
key_facts: One kW of solar in Lahore makes about {{out.pvout_year|int}} units a year, but far more in spring than in the foggy winter or the monsoon, so the same system gives a surplus in some months and a shortfall in others.

Sizing from one bill misleads: the default home's lowest bill ({{out.low_month|raw}}) suggests {{out.kw_from_low_bill|2}} kW and its highest ({{out.high_month|raw}}) suggests {{out.kw_from_high_bill|2}} kW.

Sized for the whole year, {{out.installed_kw|2}} kW makes {{out.solar_pct|int}}% of the year's units, but under net billing you still buy {{out.grid_units_year|int}} units at night and export {{out.export_units_year|int}} by day; in {{out.months_short|int}} months it makes fewer units than you use.
Covering the hardest month ({{out.peak_month|raw}}) would need {{out.kw_peak|2}} kW; under net billing the extra winter surplus earns only the buyback rate of {{out.buyback_rs|rs2}} a unit.

formula.text: kW for the year = Σ monthly units ÷ Σ monthly units per kW of solar
lines: Units per kW of solar for each month = Global Solar Atlas PV output for the city (kWh per kWp in that month)
kW for the hardest month = the largest of (month's units ÷ month's units per kW)

Solar in a month = system kW × that month's units per kW; used straight from solar = the smaller of solar and units × daylight share; bought from the grid = units − used straight; exported = solar − used straight

sections.h2: Why one electricity bill gives the wrong solar size
p: Most solar calculators divide one month's units by thirty and by the yearly average sun hours. That works only when every month looks alike. A home with ACs uses {{out.high_units|int}} units in {{out.high_month|raw}} and {{out.low_units|int}} in {{out.low_month|raw}}, so the answer swings from {{out.kw_from_low_bill|2}} kW to {{out.kw_from_high_bill|2}} kW depending on which bill you pick up.

The sun changes too. In {{out.city_name|raw}} one kW makes about {{out.peak_pvout|int}} units in {{out.peak_month|raw}} but more in {{out.best_month|raw}}, because of haze, fog or monsoon cloud. Using all twelve months removes both guesses.

sections.h2: How net billing splits each month
p: For each month the calculator multiplies the system size by that month's PV output for your city. Panels only run by day, so only the share of your use that happens in daylight ({{out.day_share|pct}} by default, as on the Home Power Planner) comes straight from them. The rest of your use is bought from the grid at your slab rate, and the daytime surplus is exported at the buyback rate.

With {{out.installed_kw|2}} kW the default home uses {{out.self_used_year|int}} units straight from the panels, buys {{out.grid_units_year|int}} units and exports {{out.export_units_year|int}} units a year. Because bought units cost more than exported units earn, a system that makes as many units as you use still leaves a bill; a battery or more daytime use lowers it.

sections.h2: Should you size solar for summer or for the whole year?
p: Sizing for the hardest month ({{out.kw_peak|2}} kW here) leaves large surpluses in the months with more sun and less use. Under net billing each exported unit earns the buyback rate, {{out.buyback_rs|rs2}} in our default, while a unit bought from the grid costs your slab rate, so oversizing for summer pays back slowly.

Sizing for the year is the usual compromise. If your sanctioned load allows it and the summer bill is the problem, test a size between the two in Advanced settings and look at the months short and the units exported.

sections.h2: Where to find your twelve months of units
p: Pakistani electricity bills print a history of the last twelve months of units next to the current reading. Copy each month into its box. If a month is missing, enter the same month from an older bill or your best estimate.
Use units, not rupees: the rupee amount changes with slabs, taxes and the FPA, while the units are what the panels have to make.

mistakes: Sizing from the summer bill alone. It gives the biggest system and the largest winter surplus, sold back at the low buyback rate.
Sizing from a winter bill. The system then falls well short from May to September, when units and bills are highest.
Using the yearly average sun hours for every month. December and July make far fewer units per kW than April.
Entering rupees instead of units. The bill amount includes slabs, taxes and the FPA; solar is sized on units.
safety: A solar system on the roof and its grid connection must be installed by a licensed electrician or an AEDB-certified installer, and net billing needs your DISCO's approval and a sanctioned load at least as large as the system.

faq.q: How do I calculate solar system size from my electricity bill?
faq.a: Add the units of all twelve months on the bill and divide by what one kW of solar makes in your city in a year, then round up to whole panels. The default Lahore home uses {{out.annual_units|int}} units a year: {{out.kw_annual|2}} kW, which is {{out.panels|int}} panels or {{out.installed_kw|2}} kW.

faq.q: Why do different calculators give such different solar sizes for my home?
faq.a: Most use one bill. The default home's bills suggest anything from {{out.kw_from_low_bill|2}} kW to {{out.kw_from_high_bill|2}} kW depending on the month; twelve months give one answer.

faq.q: Will my solar system cover my bill in July?
faq.a: Usually not fully when it is sized for the year. In the default example {{out.worst_month|raw}} is {{out.worst_short_units|int}} units short of what the panels make, because use is high and monsoon cloud lowers output; night use is bought from the grid in every month.

faq.q: Is it worth sizing solar for the summer peak?
faq.a: Only if you accept a large winter surplus. Covering {{out.peak_month|raw}} needs {{out.kw_peak|2}} kW in the default example, and the extra units in other months earn only the buyback rate.

faq.q: Does this include the battery for night use?
faq.a: No. Night use is bought from the grid under net billing. For backup at night or in loadshedding, size a battery with the solar battery calculator.

faq.q: Where is the twelve-month history on my bill?
faq.a: Pakistani DISCO bills print the units of the past twelve months in a small table, usually next to the meter readings. Copy each month into its box.
